title: Damien of Molokai (1840–1889)
hook: a Belgian priest serves the leprosy settlement on Molokai and, tradition says, begins his sermons we lepers

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bernadette in the convent, the broom after the sweeping. Your line was put back in the corner. What did you do that nobody heard about? Today, a priest who went where people were sent away. Day eight hundred ninety-two.

On the island of Molokai, in Hawaii, a flat green peninsula sits at the foot of tall sea cliffs. Sea in front, a wall of rock behind. The Hawaiian kingdom sent people with leprosy there, by law, to live apart. Families were split on the docks. Once you were sent, you were not expected to come back. A young priest from Belgium, already working on the islands, offers to go. He lands with very little. Tradition says that for years his sermons began my brethren. Then, one Sunday, they began with two different words.
screen: `A PENINSULA UNDER THE CLIFFS.` → `SENT AWAY, BY LAW.` → `A PRIEST OFFERS TO GO.`

segments.voice: His name was Jozef De Veuster. In religious life he took the name Damien, as a member of the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts. The Church now calls him Saint Damien of Molokai. Take his years there in order. First, the work. The settlement on the Kalaupapa peninsula needed everything. Damien dressed wounds. He built houses and helped build a church. He dug graves and made coffins, because people were dying and someone had to bury them with dignity. He organized care for orphaned children. Second, the nearness. He did not keep a careful distance. He ate with the people, shared his pipe, touched the sick. In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus describes the Son of man welcoming those who cared for him: "sick, and you visited me." In the Latin of the Vulgate, sick is infirmus. Damien took the visiting part to its end. Third, the two words. In time Damien found that he had the disease himself. Tradition says that from then on, he began his sermons not my brethren, but we lepers. No longer one who visits. One of them. Fourth, the end. He kept working as long as he could, and he died on Molokai, among the people he had come to serve. A word about the word. Leprosy is what the disease was called then, and it is in the saint's own sentence. Today it is called Hansen's disease, and it can be cured. Some people who have lived with it have asked not to be called lepers, and his line is honored as his, not as a label for anyone else.
screen: `DRESSING WOUNDS, BUILDING COFFINS.` · `SICK, AND YOU VISITED ME.` · `FROM MY BRETHREN TO WE LEPERS.` · `HE DIED AMONG THEM.` · then, large: `WE LEPERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand with the excluded, for two minutes in your mind first. Settle, and breathe. Who is sent to the edge where you live? Someone sick, someone old and alone, someone everyone avoids at work or school. Let one face come to mind. Don't fix anything. Just stand beside them, in your imagination, the way Damien stood beside the people of Kalaupapa. Notice what changes when you say we instead of they. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. If you don't, simply hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Damien of Molokai. A Belgian priest who served the leprosy settlement on the Kalaupapa peninsula, caught the disease, and died there among the people.
Your line: we lepers. Today, say we about someone you would usually call they, and do one small thing with them, not for them. Day eight hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Catholics in Hawaii keep Saint Damien's feast on May 10, and parishes and shrines named for him remember him as a friend of people with Hansen's disease.

visit once a year by boat.
fork.reveal: Damien offered to go. he stayed, caught the disease, and died there among the people.

original.note: Latin for sick, from Matthew 25:36 in the Vulgate: sick, and you visited me.

trapdoor: what you thought: Damien was a doctor who treated the sick from a safe distance.
what it means: he was a priest who lived among the people of Kalaupapa, built and buried and nursed, and caught the disease himself.
what a scholar hears: the shift tradition records, from my brethren to we lepers, marks a visitor becoming one of the people he served.

Damien sharing his pipe and eating with residents: often told; confirm.

Editor pass: replaced the repeated 'turns four ways' opener; Matthew 25 framing made accurate (the Son of man welcoming those who cared for him); 'people who lived through it' softened to 'some people who have lived with it'.

Audit (Oct 2026): when Damien arrived the main settlement was at Kalawao, on the Kalaupapa peninsula; the teach, word and match now say the settlement on the Kalaupapa peninsula rather than placing him in Kalaupapa village. Confirm.
